highlights: Settings > LLM opens with what is actually running. A status strip at the top of the tab reports the engine the app is configured to use, whether it answered, the context window it was started with against the one you configured and, on the vLLM tier, the size of its KV cache and how much of it is in use. It also says when the app is still running the engine it booted with while a different one is saved - the case that used to look like a setting that had not taken. Ollama installs get this readout for the first time.

A partial save no longer deletes the rest of your LLM settings. A request that stated only the engine selection used to replace the whole LLM section, discarding the Ollama settings with it. Regex generation then failed until the app was restarted, and the restart quietly restored the shipped values over anything that had been tuned. Every block a save leaves out - the Ollama settings, the vLLM settings, the regex settings - is now carried over from what is stored, and a save that would have had to guess is refused instead of writing half a document. If an earlier version emptied your Ollama settings, restart the app container to get a working block back, then re-enter any non-default endpoint, model or context window before saving.

The restart notice covers every change that needs one, and stays on screen. It used to appear only when the engine itself was switched. It now appears after any save that cannot take effect until the app container restarts - a model, an endpoint, a context window, an engine API key, or the regex retry and parallelism settings - and it names which of them changed. Only the engine you have selected is considered; editing the other engine's block raises no notice. The message is now a banner on the page that stays until you dismiss it, rather than a notification that disappeared after four seconds.

Regex retry attempts and parallel threads are their own setting. They were stored inside the Ollama block, where they had never belonged - they are the app's own loop bounds and apply whichever engine answers. They now live in their own place in the stored configuration, are moved there for you on first boot, and are checked when they are saved (1 to 20 attempts, 1 to 10 threads) instead of being accepted and failing later. A value outside that range left behind by an earlier version is reset to the shipped default when the page loads, so it can never block a save, and a Settings page cached from the previous version still has its retry and thread edits applied.

The engine cards describe the 1.4 reality, and warn before a switch that costs. Ollama is named as the default tier that every install ships with; vLLM is named as the shipped performance tier enabled with the vllm compose profile, which also accepts an OpenAI-compatible server of your own. Each card carries an (i) explaining what it needs. Switching a vLLM-tier server back to Ollama now says, before the click, that the roughly 20 GB Ollama model will be loaded onto the same GPU.

Settings > AI Assistant and Settings > Regex Builder follow the engine that is active. They used to show, and let you edit, Ollama's model and context window on a server whose questions were being answered by vLLM. On the vLLM tier they are now read-only, with a link to the LLM tab where that engine is configured, and the model and window they show are the ones actually in use.

The optional engine and its seed have stable container names. They are now named vllm and model-seed in both compose files, so they appear in Settings > Container Logs like every other service and can be addressed by name at the command line. A one-shot container that has finished its work and exited cleanly - which is what model-seed does on every start - now shows a neutral dot and a "finished" label instead of the red dot used for a crash, and the log view stops trying to reconnect to it.

The profile opt-in is written down where you will look for it. Both .env examples, the deployment guide and the model image guide now state the persistent form, COMPOSE_PROFILES=vllm in the project .env, beside the per-command --profile vllm. The persistent form matters on a vLLM-tier box: the update scripts do not pass --profile, so without that line they classify the engine and its seed as optional and not enabled here, and leave those containers on the old images. An existing vLLM install does not gain the line by upgrading - .env is written once at install time - so add it by hand, then docker compose up -d.

The Regex Builder says why a run produced nothing. Instead of one fixed sentence for every failure, it now reports what the best attempt actually achieved: how much of the line the pattern matched before it stopped, the character it stopped on, and how many fields it extracted. A run that came within a field of working no longer reads the same as one that never matched a byte.

Regex attempts now differ from one another. Parallel attempts use different approaches and sampling settings rather than asking the model the same thing several times, and an attempt that stops making progress changes approach instead of repeating itself. Generation is given twice the output budget, so a wide log line is no longer cut off mid-pattern. Attempts abandoned when a request ends no longer keep running in the background, and a slower attempt that succeeds is used rather than discarded. Pressing Generate again after a failure no longer reproduces the identical failure: the sampling is seeded per request.

Every generation attempt and one summary per request are now in the application log, so a failed run can be diagnosed from the log alone - how many attempts ran, how many distinct patterns they produced, why each one was rejected, and how far the best of them got.

New parsing examples for FortiGate and Palo Alto. Seven examples were added to the shipped example store: FortiGate key=value logs for traffic, IPS, web filter and system events, and PAN-OS lines pasted without a syslog header, including a PAN-OS 11.x line with its extra trailing fields and a WildFire file submission. They are added on first boot alongside your own examples; nothing already in the store is changed. "Train default dataset" now reports how many examples were actually added and how many were already present, instead of always reporting the file's row count.

Every reputation check now writes down what it did. One line per check records how many addresses were seen, how many were public, how many were looked up, answered or failed, and how many scored above zero and were injected into the investigation prompt - including the case where every address in the alarm was internal and nothing was looked up at all, which previously produced no line of any kind. Multicast addresses are no longer sent to AbuseIPDB: they were being counted against your API key for a result that cannot exist, and no investigation content changes as a result. Carrier-grade NAT addresses are now labelled "CGNAT (100.64/10)" instead of the misleading "reserved". If you have raised the application log level above "info", only the missing-API-key warning stays visible.

A failed alarm sync is now reported as a failure. A SIEM or database outage used to be logged as "Alarm sync complete: 0 new alarms" with a green worker card, and because the cycle counted as a success the sync circuit breaker could never open and the retry backoff never engaged. It now opens after five consecutive failures and the backoff really engages, so you will see fewer sync attempts during an outage than before. The Settings health page turns amber on the first failed cycle, names the cause and shows the last successful run, instead of staying green until the fifth. A sync that stored some alarms and refused others says so rather than reporting a clean success. Manually fetching alarms answers 503 while the SIEM is unreachable, and investigating an alarm that is not yet stored locally falls back to fetching that one alarm directly, answering 503 only when that also fails.

Compliance assessment counts the rules that really have alarm data. The count was read with a query against a table this product does not create, and the failure was suppressed, so every framework on every install reported "0 rules with data". It now uses the same evidence the coverage matrix uses, so the two agree. Expect the number to move from zero to a real value. Your compliance coverage percentage does not change - it never used this count. If the lookup ever fails, the assessment now says "unavailable" rather than printing a zero it did not measure.

Rhythm Insights imports the rule list before it scores anything. The daily batch now begins by importing the enabled AIE rules from LogRhythm, so an install that had never clicked Sync Rules stops reporting zeros. Nothing is scored on an empty inventory any more: the batch says which steps it skipped and why, instead of publishing zero coverage as if it were a measurement, and the log now reports how many of its steps actually ran. The daily sync never deletes rules: a rule that is no longer enabled in LogRhythm is marked inactive and stays on record, and a sync that comes back empty - while the SIEM is unreachable, for instance - changes nothing; only the Sync Rules button on the AI SOC page still removes rules. The daily log-source gap snapshot runs regardless of the rule inventory, because it never depended on it. Recalculate on the Rhythm Insights page syncs the rules first, so it is a one-button recovery, and a coverage step that had nothing to score is reported as skipped rather than done. On a first boot, the catch-up batch runs within a minute of the model becoming available rather than waiting for the next scheduled slot.

Fewer results lost to an unreadable model answer. The repair already applied to rule-quality assessment now also covers TDIR classification, MITRE technique classification and the AI recommendations, so an answer that arrives with a missing closing brace or a line of trailing prose is recovered instead of discarded.

The AI Assistant answers instead of thinking forever. When the model returned nothing on the fallback path, the chat streamed no text and left "Thinking..." running indefinitely. It now ends with a short message asking you to try again or rephrase - and on a coverage question cut short, with the more specific guidance that question earned. Any reply that ends without text - a connection dropped mid-answer, an error from the engine, or pressing Stop - now clears the indicator.

Threat Universe says why a deep-linked alarm has no graph. Opening an alarm from a link used to suggest widening the window or checking filters, advice that cannot help. It now names the actual reason: no evidence logs, still waiting for the backfill, older than the retention window, or not synced yet. Alarms with no evidence logs - meta and progression rules, which fire off other alarms rather than off logs - can never have a graph, and the notice offers to open the alarm in the SIEM instead. A separate timezone fault is fixed in the same place: alarm timestamps were read in the browser's local zone rather than UTC, shifting the search window by the full offset, so an alarm sitting in the graph could be reported as missing. Installs more than six hours from UTC were most affected.

Saving two Settings cards at once no longer loses one of them. Two browser tabs, two administrators, or one double-click on Save could previously write the second card over the first and silently discard the first card's section. Saves are now serialised, and config.json is replaced in a single step rather than emptied and rewritten, so a page loading - or the app restarting - at the moment of a save can no longer read a half-written configuration.

The release gate now looks where the 1.4.0 fault was hiding. The gate added in 1.4.1 walked the shipped packages with a mechanism that has to execute a package before it can see inside it, so on the broken 1.4.0 image it reported two failures and still exited zero, never naming the second upload route at all. It now lists the modules from the filesystem first and imports each one independently: on that same image it finds 130 modules, 17 import failures, and fails the cut. A dependency that leaves the image must now be listed by name with the release and the reason it went, or the gate refuses to pass - which is exactly the check the withdrawn release needed. The gate also runs the two start-up steps the container performs before the application starts, so a build that could not merge its configuration, migrate a stored customer document or write its certificate is caught before it is published rather than after. The gate now refuses to run without the previous image to compare against unless told so explicitly.

Upgrade note. This release changes services other than the app, so it is not eligible for the one-click upgrade in Settings > About: run the update script once and accept the docker-compose.yml replacement, which gives the optional engine and its seed their container names. On a vLLM-tier server, set COMPOSE_PROFILES=vllm in the project .env and run docker compose up -d so the engine is recreated under its stable name. Your stored configuration is migrated on first boot; rolling back to 1.4.1 leaves everything else intact but resets the regex retry attempts and parallel threads to the shipped 6 and 3, so re-enter them if you had tuned them and then come forward again. The corrected compliance "rules with data" counts appear at the next daily insights batch or a manual recalculate - there is no one-time pass on upgrade. An install whose SIEM connection is broken will now report "degraded" on the Settings health page where it previously reported "healthy"; an install with no SIEM connected at all is unchanged. And because the daily batch now imports the rule list itself, the app connects to the LogRhythm EMDB over SQL once a day rather than only when Sync Rules is clicked - a site that firewalled the app off from SQL after its one manual sync will log one connection failure a day until that is allowed or accepted.

summary: 1.4.0 is withdrawn: its app image does not start, because a dependency the form-handling routes need was missing. 1.4.1 is the release to install.
No feature changes from 1.4.0 - everything that release described is here, in an image that boots
A new release gate now imports every module and builds the application inside the image before it can be published
App-only release: one click from Settings > About on 1.4.0. From 1.3.x run the update script once; it carries the 1.4.0 compose change and lands you here in the same run.
highlights: What happened. The 1.4.0 app image cannot start. Removing the outbound n8n MCP tools mode took two packages out of the dependency list, and python-multipart - the parser FastAPI uses for file uploads - had only ever been installed because those packages happened to pull it in. FastAPI checks for it at the moment a route that accepts an uploaded file is declared, which happens while the application is being built, so the container failed at startup and restarted in a loop rather than failing some later request. Two routes declare such an upload: training the Regex Builder's example store, and the insights import. The package is now named in its own right, where removing something else cannot take it away again. Nothing else about the release changed: 1.4.1 is 1.4.0 plus that one dependency and the gate below. If you installed 1.4.0, move to 1.4.1; if you have not, install 1.4.1 directly.

A release gate that starts the thing before we ship it. The reason this reached you is worth saying plainly: every check the release process had reads a FILE out of the image - the version, the update script, the release notes - and a file reads perfectly well inside an image that cannot boot. The unit tests all passed, on machines that happened to have the missing package. There is now a gate that runs against the built image itself: it imports every module the product ships, inside the container, on the same paths the app uses; it builds the application object there and requires the expected set of endpoints to be present, the upload route among them; and it prints the full list of packages that changed since the previous release, so a dependency that quietly disappears is seen at cut time rather than at yours. It is part of the checklist from now on, and no image ships without it passing.

Upgrade note. This is an app-only release. On 1.4.0 use Settings > About > Upgrade now - it replaces the app container and nothing else. From 1.3.x, run the update script once: it carries the 1.4.0 compose change (the two profile-gated services for the optional engine, dormant unless you enable them) and finishes on 1.4.1 in the same run. The optional vLLM engine is unchanged from what 1.4.0 described and is still opt-in; see deploy/model-image/README.md in the release.

summary: Withdrawn - the image does not start; install 1.4.1. An optional second AI engine for 32 GB Ada-class cards — roughly twice the tokens per second, on an 8-bit artifact, chosen in Settings
The engine's weights arrive as a Docker Hub image and are unpacked into a volume by compose, with every file checked against the image's own manifest
Guardrails, the outbound n8n MCP tools mode and the Assistant's Think toggle are removed, and your saved configuration is migrated for you

Not a one-click release: run the update script and accept the docker-compose.yml replacement. It adds two services that stay dormant — the new engine starts only if you ask for it, and nothing about a standard install changes.
highlights: A second engine, for the boxes that can use it. RhythmAI has only ever spoken to Ollama. 1.4 adds an optional engine built on vLLM that serves an 8-bit AWQ build of the same RhythmAI 27B model, for customers whose GPU is an Ada-class 32 GB card. On the gated box it answered at a median 107.6 tokens per second against Ollama's 56.1 on the same prompts — the difference between reading an investigation as it is written and waiting for it. The artifact occupies 21.5 GiB on the card and leaves room for a 64k context window with an fp8 KV cache, which is what the shipped command line asks for. This is an addition, not a replacement: the Ollama path is byte-for-byte what it was, it stays the default on every install, and Ollama remains in every deployment because it also serves the embeddings the Regex Builder needs.

You choose the engine in Settings. Settings > AI Assistant carries an engine selector and a card for the engine that is active, with its endpoint, its model name and what the app's own probe found when it last checked. Switching engines is a saved setting, not a rebuild — the app reads it, checks that the engine answers, and reports what it found. Like every other LLM setting, the change takes effect after the app container restarts. If the engine is unreachable the card says so in plain language instead of failing a question later.

The model travels like everything else: as an image. The engine's weights are published as a private Docker Hub image and installed by a one-shot `model-seed` service that fills a named volume and exits; the engine mounts that volume read-only and starts only after the seed has finished. The image carries a manifest of every file's size and checksum, and the seed writes its completion marker only once each unpacked file matches, so an interrupted or corrupted seed simply starts over and the engine is never handed a half-written model. Updating the model is a tag bump: the seed refills the volume and the engine is recreated onto the new weights. There is no second set of credentials, no hand-placed folder and no separate download channel — one `docker login`, then `docker compose --profile vllm up -d`. `docker save` still covers an air-gapped box. Keep the model image after seeding: it is what refills the volume without a pull if the volume is ever lost. Full instructions, including the offline path and the disk it needs, are in deploy/model-image/README.md inside the release.

Three features leave the product. Guardrails, the second-model check on AI Assistant chat, is removed: it needed its own ~20 GB safeguard model beside the 27B, which a single 32 GB card cannot hold, so it shipped disabled and stayed disabled. The outbound n8n MCP tools mode is removed: n8n left the shipped stack in May 2026, so the toggle in the Assistant toolbar had no server to reach and produced a confusing failure instead of an answer. The Assistant's Think toggle is removed: it set a flag no backend code ever read, because reasoning is baked into the model's weights. The inbound LogRhythm skill store is a different feature and is untouched. Your saved configuration is migrated on first boot: the three retired sections are dropped from the stored document, so a support bundle no longer shows a feature that is not there. Nothing else in your settings is touched.

Builds are reproducible again. The image pins its entire Python dependency set to the versions that shipped in 1.3.3, in a constraints file checked in beside the requirements. This also repaired the build outright: a new release of one transitive library had started to win over the copy that comes with the base operating system, and that copy cannot be replaced, so every image build had been failing at the dependency step. Nothing in the running product changes — the image now contains the versions it was tested with, and a rebuild of the same commit produces the same image.

Upgrade note. This release changes services other than the app, so it is not eligible for the one-click upgrade in Settings > About: run the update script once and accept the docker-compose.yml replacement when it offers it. The new compose defines two extra services, `vllm` and `model-seed`, behind a profile. On a standard install that profile is off, both services stay dormant, and your stack starts exactly as it did on 1.3.3 — the update touches the app and nothing else. The new engine is opt-in and is a deliberate piece of work: a Docker Hub login for the model image, `--profile vllm` on your compose commands, the engine selected in Settings, and an app restart. Read deploy/model-image/README.md before you start; it lists the GPU, the disk and the steps in order.

summary: Series of events: an arrow written inside a step no longer splits it into broken halves

highlights: Series of events keeps steps whole. The model sometimes writes a connection inside one step, such as "HTTP PUT 192.0.2.13 → 203.0.113.10:80", and the chain splitter cut on that inner arrow, leaving two broken chips with stray brackets and a technique chip on a fragment. Bracketed steps are now read as whole units: an arrow inside a step is text, and only the arrows between steps separate them. Chains without brackets behave exactly as before.

summary: Series of events: every step names its technique, repeated rules are merged, and long chains fold to eight steps with a "+N more" control

highlights: Series of events reads as a timeline again. When an alarm sits inside hundreds of correlated alarms the 27B lists every rule it saw, sometimes twice, and sometimes as a bare technique ID with a count. Three rendering fixes: a step that carries only an ID and a count now shows the technique name from the report's own MITRE table ("Command & Scripting Interpreter ×2" rather than an empty chip with "×2"); the same rule listed twice is merged into one step with the counts summed; and a chain longer than eight steps shows the first eight with a "+N more" control that expands the rest, so a dense chain stays readable in the side panel without hiding anything.

Upgrade note. App-only: on 1.3.0 or 1.3.1 use Settings > About > Upgrade now. From any earlier version run the update script once; it carries the 1.3.0 runtime and model changes and finishes on 1.3.2 in the same run.

summary: Investigation reports say what they are doing during the one pause analysts notice ("Checking anomalies…")
Update script: stalled model downloads are detected by rate, with percent and speed on every progress line, and the Windows script's damaged-download check now actually runs
Quieter, truer boot log after an upgrade: the model check re-probes instead of warning too early, and the migration-revision notice is reconciled once
App-only release: one click from Settings > About on 1.3.0. Customers on older versions run the update script once and land here directly, including the 27B model step from 1.3.0.
highlights: Checking anomalies. The 27B writes a few sentences under the Threat Analysis table that the report deliberately does not show, and while it writes them the screen used to sit still for several seconds before the Anomalies section appeared. During exactly that gap the report now shows a small pulsing "Checking anomalies…" label at the end of the text, so the pause reads as work in progress rather than a stall. Every other section streams as before; the label appears only where the pause is.

Model download watchdog measures rate, not silence. On the 1.3.0 update a 19.5 GB model download crawled at a few megabytes a minute after the content network dropped one part, and the previous watchdog, which only reacted to a download that had stopped completely, never fired. Both update scripts now judge progress by bytes gained over the last six minutes and restart the Ollama runtime when that falls below 64 MB, resuming from the parts already on disk. Progress lines show the total, the percentage and the current speed, and a restart is announced in plain language with what is kept.

Windows updater: the damaged-download safety net now runs. The check that discards a corrupt partial download before resuming was handed to the container through a quoting path that Windows PowerShell 5.1 mangles, so on Windows it silently never ran. It is now delivered intact on PowerShell 5.1 and 7, verified against a throwaway container. The Linux script was unaffected.

Boot log after an upgrade. The update recreates the app before it installs the new model, so the first boot used to warn that the model was missing and never said when it arrived. The app now notes that the model is not present yet and re-checks for up to an hour, logging once when it is installed; the warning is kept only for the case where it never appears. A one-time notice about migration 002 having been revised since it was applied is now reconciled once instead of repeated on every boot.

Upgrade note. This is an app-only release: on 1.3.0 use Settings > About > Upgrade now. From any earlier version run the update script once; it carries the 1.3.0 runtime and model changes and finishes on 1.3.1 in the same run. Refresh the script from the image when it tells you to.

summary: New RhythmAI 27B model — one model now answers investigations AND writes regex
Compliance matching rebuilt on LogRhythm's own rule definitions and pack rosters
Ollama runtime moves from 0.20.6 to 0.32.14 (compose change)
Not a one-click release: run the update script, accept the docker-compose.yml replacement, and allow time for a ~19.5 GB model download
highlights: One model, two jobs — RhythmAI 27B. Investigations, the AI Assistant, coverage and compliance analysis and the Regex Builder now all run on a single fine-tuned model, RhythmAI:27b. It replaces both the 9B that answered chat and the separate qwen2.5-coder:32b that wrote regex — one model to keep resident, one set of prompts, one thing to upgrade. On the standard security batteries it scores CyberMetric-500 93.8% (the 9B scored 83.6%), CTIBench threat-intelligence multiple-choice 72.0% — GPT-4 level on that battery — and SecEval 74.8%. On our own regex battery it writes a correct pattern 84.6% of the time against the retired coder model's 38.5%, which is what made the consolidation possible rather than merely convenient. Reasoning stays baked into the fine-tuned weights: short or absent think blocks are the intended behavior, not degradation.

Ollama runtime moves to 0.32.14. The 27B needs a newer inference runtime than the 9B did, so the shipped compose moves the pin from ollama/ollama:0.20.6 to ollama/ollama:0.32.14 and adds two settings a model this size needs. OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=-1 keeps it resident — Ollama's default unloads an idle model after five minutes, which would turn the first question of every morning into a multi-minute cold load. OLLAMA_LOAD_TIMEOUT=15m gives a ~20 GB load from a slow disk room to finish instead of failing the request outright. Both pins stay explicit — never 'latest'. Because this release changes a service other than the app, it is NOT eligible for the one-click upgrade in Settings > About; see the upgrade note below.

Compliance matching now reads LogRhythm's own rule definitions. Framework coverage used to be inferred from rule names and drilldown text, which credited rules that merely sounded relevant and missed rules doing the work under a different name. It now matches in three layers: your LogRhythm Knowledge Base's compliance pack rosters (authoritative — the console's own answer to which rules belong to a pack, and it credits the rules that belong to several packs at once), definition fingerprints built from each AIE rule's actual field logic, and the old drilldown-text match only as a last resort. Results are reported in two tiers instead of one number: STRONG matches (the rule's strongest specified component and its name lineage both agree, and the rule's shape fits) and CANDIDATE matches (plausible, listed separately, never silently counted toward your score). A new card calls out rules that are PRESENT in your deployment but DISABLED — the most common reason a framework scores lower than expected — and rule filters now show rule names throughout instead of numeric rule IDs.

Compliance expected-rule lists now come from your LogRhythm KB packs. For every framework the assessment finds the matching KB module on your SIEM and uses its rule roster as the expected list when the pack is installed; our reference lists remain the fallback. Frameworks whose pack is not installed are now shown as "rule pack not installed" instead of as rules to write. Coverage percentages can change on the first assessment after this upgrade because the denominators now match the vendor packs (for example CIS Controls and NCSC CAF); the tab states which list each framework uses.

27B integration fixes from field testing. Five issues surfaced by running the new model against real customer data, all fixed: a repeat penalty carried over from the 9B era corrupted entity names in long reports (hostnames and usernames came back subtly misspelled) and is now neutral for this model; the Regex Builder could loop on very long CSV log lines and now caps its output; alarm drilldown was dropping the 'group' field on its way to the model, so group membership (a user being in Domain Admins, for instance) was invisible in reports that should have cited it; the drilldown backfill worker logged 'Queued N' where N counted rows it had merely CHECKED rather than queued, and now reports the measured outcome; and report headers came back in Arabic when the source log contained Arabic text.

Regex Builder examples for Palo Alto and long CSV logs. The Regex Builder retrieves similar worked examples before it drafts a pattern, and that corpus contained no Palo Alto seeds at all — one of the most common firewall log formats in the field — and nothing long enough to teach it how wide comma-separated logs are structured. Both are now seeded, which is what first-attempt quality on those formats depends on. Regex Builder examples now persist across upgrades and are seeded automatically at startup: the vector store moved onto its own Docker volume, so it is no longer wiped every time the app container is recreated.

Upgrade note: this release changes the compose file AND downloads a new model, so it is not a one-click upgrade. Run Update-RhythmAI.ps1 (Windows) or update-rhythmai.sh (Linux), and ANSWER YES when it offers to replace your docker-compose.yml — that replacement carries the Ollama runtime change, and declining it leaves the new model unable to run. The script then downloads RhythmAI:27b, about 19.5 GB: allow time (30–90 minutes is normal, longer on a slow link) and keep roughly 20 GB free on the Docker volume for the duration of the swap. Only once the new model is verified in place does the script remove the ones it supersedes (RhythmAI:9b and the qwen2.5-coder:32b regex model), so the net disk change is about -6 GB; the embedding model all-minilm:l6-v2 is kept. If the download fails, nothing is removed and your existing models keep working — re-run the script, or use Settings > AI Assistant > Download in the app. The GPU requirement is unchanged: 32 GB VRAM minimum.

summary: Threat Universe AI analysis now tells the full incident story

highlights: Threat Universe — full incident narratives. "Analyze with AI" on an entity or triage brief now produces a structured incident story — what happened, in what order, across which stages — instead of a short statistics recap. Roughly 8x more analytical content per analysis, verified against structure and grounding gates.

Alarm rule sync fixed at multi-engine sites. If your deployment assigns AIE rules to more than one engine, the Settings > Rule Quality "Sync Alarms" button failed with a database conflict on every click (rules deployed to N engines returned N duplicate rows). The sync now de-duplicates and is fully idempotent — the first sync after upgrading also repairs a previously partial rule table automatically.

Log Source Coverage counts accepted sources only. LogRhythm's acceptance queue proposes log source types by signature-matching incoming streams, and those pending (never-accepted) records — which can never receive logs — previously appeared in coverage as sources "without logs in 24h/7d", sometimes under vendor names you never deployed. Coverage and health scoring now count Active sources only.
Upgrade note: app-only release — installs on 1.2.28 can upgrade with one click from Settings > About. API consumers: no endpoint changes.

summary: Accurate cross-pull counts on the graph canvas
Release notes now reach every install
Update script waits properly on slow first boots
No action required
highlights: Honest counts when pulls overlap. In the Threat Universe, a host, user or IP that appears in SEVERAL pulls' activity used to display the SUM of each pull's count — but pulls in one investigation typically capture the same underlying log events from different angles, so the sum double-counted shared events (a real case: two IP pulls each saw the same 168 events and the canvas printed ×336, a number that exists nowhere in the SIEM). Satellites now reconcile across pulls: when every contributing pull stored its complete log set, the label shows the exact deduplicated event count ('×168 · 2 pulls'); when exactness is impossible (older cached pulls, very large pulls), it shows the strongest single pull's count as an honest floor ('×168+ · 2 pulls') — never a fabricated total. The AI assistant's per-artifact answers were always deduplicated correctly; the canvas now agrees with it. Pulls cached before 1.2.26 lack the per-log identity fields needed for exact reconciliation and use the floor until refreshed.

Release notes and one-click eligibility for NEWER versions now reach every install. The update check previously tried to fetch release metadata from a location that has been inaccessible since day one, silently falling back to the release notes bundled inside your installed image — which by definition never describe versions newer than yours. Metadata now lives at a public channel (github.com/imeta-exabeam/rhythmai-releases) that is updated with every release, so the Update Available card can show you what a new version contains BEFORE you install it, and the Upgrade-now button can verify eligibility without workarounds.

Update script polish from the first customer-site run. The health wait at the end of the update scripts polls the app container's own Docker healthcheck instead of probing HTTPS from the host (same signal Docker itself uses; immune to host-side TLS quirks), and allows five minutes instead of two — a first boot after a multi-release jump runs configuration merge, schema migrations and seeding, which legitimately outlasted the old deadline on customer hardware while the upgrade itself had succeeded.

No database migration and no compose change from 1.2.27. App-image-only: if you are on 1.2.27 with the updater sidecar, Settings → About → Upgrade now applies it (note: the 1.2.27 update check reads only its bundled metadata, so if the button does not light up, run the update script once more — from 1.2.28 onward the public channel makes the button reliable). The Ollama pin (0.20.6), RhythmAI:9b model, prompts and context budgets are unchanged.

Update script now ships inside the app image
No action required
highlights: One update script for every customer, span-aware. The customer update scripts (Update-RhythmAI.ps1 / update-rhythmai.sh) now read the release metadata shipped in the new image, work out which services actually changed between YOUR running version and the target — across however many releases you are jumping — and pull/recreate only those. Upgrading across an app-only stretch touches the app container alone; a stretch that includes, say, the 1.2.24 log-proxy addition touches exactly the app and that sidecar; databases and the AI engine are left running unless a release genuinely changed them. Whenever the metadata cannot vouch for the whole span (very old versions, custom compose files missing a service), the script falls back to the full-stack behavior it always had — it fails open, never wrong. It also tells you which services it chose and why.

The update script distributes itself. Both scripts now ship inside the app image at /app/deploy/, so any deployment can always extract the current one (docker run --rm --entrypoint cat rhythmai/rhythmai:latest /app/deploy/update-rhythmai.sh > update-rhythmai.sh — same for the .ps1). A script you already have checks its own version against the copy in the new image and prominently tells you when a newer one is available. No more wondering whether your updater is current.

No database migration and no compose change from 1.2.26. This release is app-image-only — if you are already on 1.2.26 with the updater sidecar, it is the first release you can apply with the Upgrade now button in Settings → About. The Ollama pin (0.20.6), RhythmAI:9b model, prompts and context budgets are unchanged.

summary: Upgrade RhythmAI straight from Settings
Threat Universe captures far more log detail
Process lineage: see what spawned what
Scannable release notes with full-detail view
Compose file update required — use the update script
highlights: One-click upgrades from the browser. When a new app-only release is available, Settings → About now shows an 'Upgrade now' button next to the release notes: confirm, watch the download and restart progress live, and the page reloads on the new version — no SSH, no docker commands. The work is done by a new single-purpose 'updater' sidecar container that holds the Docker socket so the app itself never has to: it accepts exactly one kind of request (swap the app container's image, pinned to the rhythmai/rhythmai repository, forward-only, token-authenticated over an isolated internal network with no published ports), recreates the app with its exact volumes, networks and environment, health-checks the new version for up to 3 minutes, and if it fails to come up healthy AUTOMATICALLY RESTORES the previous version — keeping the failed container for support diagnosis. After any upgrade a 'Roll back' control can return to the previously recorded version the same way. Releases that change the deployment itself (like this one) are never offered one-click: the button only appears when every release between your version and the latest is marked app-only, so a UI upgrade can never half-apply a release. Deployments without the sidecar keep the familiar copy-the-command flow, now corrected to include the '-p rhythmai' project name (running the documented command without it created a second, parallel stack instead of updating the existing one). The upgrade endpoints require the Settings permission and every trigger is recorded in the audit trail.

Threat Universe sees the whole log. Data Indexer pulls previously kept 24 fields per log; they now keep 82 of the 105 LogRhythm provides — process lineage (parent process: 'powershell.exe (parent: winword.exe)' now appears in evidence rows and the AI's analysis where before the parent was invisible), session and logon type, action outcomes (status/result/reason), geographic and zone context, MAC addresses, entity topology, transfer volumes, user agents and more. The raw log BODY is still never stored. Alongside the widening, three data-quality fixes: host activity now reads the fields LogRhythm actually populates (some environments send hostnames in fields the graph previously ignored, so machines that appeared in logs never appeared as computers — they do now, with honest per-log counting), Active Directory object names (cn=...) no longer masquerade as computers, and an IP that arrives in a hostname field is shown once as an IP instead of twice as an IP plus a phantom computer. NOTE: pulls cached before this release gain the new fields when refreshed (the ⟳ button) or when their 60-minute cache expires.

Clearer canvas labels under spotlight. Spotlighting an artifact from the Top Alarms rail now names every alarm in the lit cluster (when 30 or fewer are lit), and zooming in close names alarms regardless — the busy-canvas protection that keeps hundreds of labels from smearing stays in force everywhere else.

Release notes built for scanning. The Update Available card now shows a few short bullets per release — what changed and whether any action is needed — with a 'Full release notes' toggle per release for the complete details you are reading now.

No database migration — but the compose file changes this release: it adds the updater sidecar service, its isolated internal network, its state volume, and an UPDATER_TOKEN secret in .env (the update scripts generate the token automatically if missing). Use the customer update script (Update-RhythmAI.ps1 / update-rhythmai.sh) — it shows you the compose diff and asks before replacing; the image also ships the reference compose at /app/deploy/docker-compose.yml. A deployment that declines the sidecar loses nothing it has today: the About page simply keeps the manual update command. The Ollama pin (0.20.6), RhythmAI:9b model, prompts and context budgets are unchanged.

summary: Richer evidence behind Analyze with AI
Background AI work now runs once daily
New Neo4j graph stats in Settings
No action required
highlights: Graph Assistant — the AI now sees what the analyst sees. The Analyze-with-AI context was rebuilt as a budgeted, unit-tested evidence pipeline: up to 40 deep raw-log rows per artifact (from the 200 already cached per pull, fairly divided as pulls grow — total prompt cost stays constant no matter how many artifacts you assemble), the previously invisible evidence families (ports, URLs, file hashes, commands/actions, log sources), per-artifact honesty stamps (exact vs sampled counts, cache age — 'pulled 6d ago' — and a note that row times are event times), alarm links carrying risk and MITRE technique, and — when Analyze is clicked from a triage brief — the brief's own findings (scope, timeline, blast radius, hostile reputation) attached as narrative material. The kill-chain stage menu now reads only marker-fenced pulled evidence, so brief text can never unlock empty stages. Verified by a 60-run before/after evaluation on live data: the enriched build eliminated the baseline's watchdog trips and think-fallbacks entirely, every sampled claim traced verbatim to the evidence, latency within 1.22x, and answers now name real objects (documents, status fields) while stating honest negatives ('no direct lateral movement observed') instead of asserting unsourced movement.

Smarter suggested questions. Follow-up chips are minted only when their backing data actually exists in your pulls — firewall-heavy environments get port and flow chips, EDR-heavy get hashes and commands, proxy-heavy get URLs and domains — and a reputation chip appears when a triage brief with hostile AbuseIPDB findings rode the analysis. Time, reputation, adjacency and alarm-severity questions automatically use the full evidence context while keeping the short answer format. Chip answers are 3x faster, and the stray consulting-style closers and table dumps are gone.

Background Work — a new Settings section that keeps the GPU for analysts. Automatic incident creation (AI SOC) is now OFF by default: previously, background workers grouped alarms into incidents and generated an AI title for every cluster around the clock, regardless of the per-rule auto-investigate toggles — the LLM burn ran even with everything switched off. Incidents can always be created manually or via API, and the AI SOC page explains the state. API NOTE: with the switch off, POST /api/incidents/auto-generate returns 200 with disabled:true and creates nothing. Rhythm Insights background analytics (SIEM syncs, rule classification, quality assessment, coverage recalculation, summaries) now run as ONE daily batch at a configurable server-UTC time (default midnight) instead of 5-minute/hourly/daily timers — AI steps stand down while an analyst chat, MITRE classify, or manual recalculation is in flight, a failed step waits for tomorrow instead of retrying every 5 minutes (this fixes a latent defect where one failing step could re-run the heavy AI block continuously), and a missed window waits for the next slot rather than storming the GPU at boot. Every Run-Now button still works for on-demand freshness. The card shows server time, last run and next run.

Assistant readability and branding. Dark mode now mirrors light mode's hierarchy: emphasized topic terms use the blue accent (they previously rendered red, which mis-signals threat), suggested-question chips are bright text on a properly visible pill, and risk levels keep their meaningful colors. The assistant also now carries exactly one logo — the theme-aware RhythmAI wordmark — replacing a stale LogRhythm icon that had survived in four places, and the duplicate per-message avatar is gone.

Neo4j graph visibility. Settings → Database gains a 'Neo4j graph' tile (total nodes and relationships) and a Graph Contents list — node counts by label and relationship counts by type — so the store that grows with your Threat Universe window is finally observable next to the PostgreSQL tables. Counts come from Neo4j's count store (milliseconds, no scan); if Neo4j is unreachable the section reads 'unavailable' without affecting the page. Store byte-size is intentionally omitted on Community edition, which exposes no honest source for it.

No database migration and no compose change from 1.2.24. Pull the 1.2.25 app image and recreate the app container; the new configuration keys (aiSoc, insights schedule) merge in automatically with safe defaults on first boot. Cadence notes for operators: new-rule classification and SIEM metadata syncs now refresh in the daily batch (or on demand via Run Now) instead of every 5-60 minutes. The Ollama pin (0.20.6), RhythmAI:9b model, prompts and context budgets are unchanged.

summary: Live container logs in the browser
One-click support diagnostics bundle
User management now lives in Settings
Compose file update required — use the update script
highlights: Live Container Logs in the browser. Settings → Health Check gains a 'Container Logs' tab that streams the live logs of every RhythmAI container (app, postgres, neo4j, ollama) straight into the browser — no SSH, no docker commands. Pick a container from the rail (with live up/health state), watch the tail follow in real time, pause and resume, search with in-line highlighting, toggle timestamps, expand to full screen, and download a deeper tail as a file. Lines are colour-coded by the log's own severity (red for ERROR/FATAL, amber for warnings, with a legend) rather than by which stream they arrived on. If a container restarts mid-stream the viewer reconnects on its own and says so. Access is read-only by construction: the app talks to a new 'socket-proxy' sidecar (tecnativa/docker-socket-proxy) that exposes ONLY read endpoints of the Docker API — no start/stop/exec, POST disabled, the Docker socket mounted read-only, confined to an internal network only the app can reach, and never published on a host port. The app itself never touches the Docker socket. Log viewing is permission-gated (Settings access), audited, and secret-masked; deployments that skip the sidecar simply see a setup panel with the compose snippet instead.

One-click support diagnostics. Settings → Health Check also gains a 'Diagnostics' tab that replaces 'run this script on the server and email us the output': press Start, reproduce the problem, press Stop, download a single zip and attach it to your support ticket. The bundle captures container states and restart counts, per-container logs from exactly the capture window, RhythmAI's own file logs sliced to the window, health-check and Ollama snapshots (before/after), database table counts and migration state, container-to-SIEM connectivity socket tests, and a redacted copy of the configuration. Redaction is enforced, not promised: passwords, keys, tokens and secret values are scrubbed by a recursive allowlist-plus-entropy pass, the zip's manifest honestly lists the few host-only items an in-app bundle cannot include (GPU nvidia-smi, host disk/RAM, installer logs), and optional verbose capture bumps logging to DEBUG for the session only — it never persists. AI reasoning traces are excluded by default and require an explicit opt-in checkbox, since they can contain alarm content from your SIEM. Every diagnostic session is audited (started, stopped, downloaded).

User Management moves into Settings — and the user/role APIs are properly locked down. The standalone Users app card is gone; user and role administration now lives where administration belongs: Settings → Users, with the same Users/Roles views inside (old /users bookmarks redirect automatically, and roles created in the Roles tab appear in the Add User picker immediately). Under the hood this release closes a real authorization gap: the /users and /roles APIs previously required only a valid login, so ANY authenticated account could list, create or modify users — including resetting another account's password — by calling the API directly. All user and role administration endpoints now require the Users permission. Changing a password follows an identity rule: you can always change YOUR OWN password (self-service and the forced-change-at-first-login flow are untouched for every role), while changing someone else's requires the Users permission; the force-reset flag only takes effect for permission holders, denied attempts on another account's password are recorded in the audit trail as authz.denied, and the audit trail now correctly distinguishes self-service password changes from administrator resets. NOTE for automation: if you script user provisioning against the API, the service account running those scripts must now hold a role with the Users permission — previously any account worked, which was the hole. Custom roles keep exactly the access they had: a role with only the Users permission still reaches user management (the Settings page shows it just the Users section), and a role with only Settings access no longer sees user management it couldn't reach before.

Data Indexer health — pick your window, and a cache honesty fix. The Data Indexer tab now has a 24 hours / 48 hours / 72 hours / 7 days selector, and the summary tiles follow the selected window (previously both were fixed to 24 hours, so a quiet day read as 'no SIEM load at all' even when the history had activity). Windows are also labeled in plain words ('7 days', not '168h'). Behind it, a cache-poisoning bug is fixed: a user-artifact pull runs two SIEM searches (login and account fields), and when one of them timed out while the other legitimately returned zero, the pull was cached as a confident 'exact 0 events' — analysts then saw 'no activity' for an artifact that had plenty. A pull that partially fails now either reports its results as inexact or fails outright; it never caches a false zero.

Threat Universe investigation fixes. Deep links from Alarm Investigation now build their time window in the alarm's local time — SIEM alarm timestamps were being parsed as UTC, which shifted the self-heal window by the UTC offset and could miss the alarm entirely (and skewed the auto-picked window preset). Case notes created from a story-mode analysis now carry the full narrative analysis instead of whatever the last short follow-up answer happened to be. Follow-up answers no longer inherit a '✅ Next' checklist from earlier answers in the conversation.

Quieter, cleaner logs — visible now that you can see them. The app's startup no longer attempts a legacy database index that has failed on every boot since the data model changed (multiple log sources legitimately share a type); postgres logs are free of the recurring 'could not create unique index' ERROR block that every deployment has been accumulating silently. Container log output across services is also bounded in compose (json-file rotation, 50 MB × 5 per service), so logs can no longer grow without limit on the host.

No database migration — but the compose file changes this release. Pull the 1.2.24 app image and recreate the app container. To get Container Logs and full Diagnostics, add the new socket-proxy sidecar and logs-net network from the reference compose — the customer update scripts (shipped since 1.2.23) detect the compose change, show you the diff, and ask before replacing; the image also ships the reference compose at /app/deploy/docker-compose.yml. A deployment that declines the sidecar loses nothing it has today: Container Logs shows a setup panel, Diagnostics still produces a bundle with the container-level sections marked unavailable, and everything else works. The Ollama pin (0.20.6), RhythmAI:9b model, prompts and context budgets are unchanged.

summary: Audit trail for every analyst action
New Data Indexer health tab
Threat Universe answers now cite real evidence
No action required
highlights: Enterprise audit telemetry — RhythmAI now records its own activity. Every analyst action inside the app (logins and login failures with a reason, logouts, permission denials, user and role administration, configuration and secret changes, AI investigations, Data-Indexer pulls, triage briefs, reputation checks, AI analyses, case creation, and skill/MCP approvals and executions) is written as an audit event: always to a local rotating trail at logs/audit.log (one JSON object per line, 50 MB × 5 backups) and, when configured, forwarded to your SIEM as standard RFC 5424 syslog over UDP or TCP. Configure it under Settings → Audit & Telemetry: master switch, syslog host, port, protocol and facility, plus a 'Send test event' button that reports each sink's result. Ingest it either way — point a syslog source at the collector, or have a LogRhythm agent file-monitor logs/audit.log (the compose file now mounts it on the host). Audit emission is fully non-blocking and can never slow or fail an analyst request; passwords, tokens, API keys, secret values and LLM prompt/response bodies are never written — configuration and secret events carry key NAMES only.

Data Indexer health — evidence of what RhythmAI asks of your SIEM. Settings → Health Check gains a 'Data Indexer' tab listing recent Threat Universe pulls with the analyst who ran each one, the artifact queried, the time window, whether it was served from cache or hit the Data Indexer live, how many logs came back, and how long the live query took (colour-coded), plus a 24-hour summary of live versus cache-served pulls with median and slowest query times. Built so a customer question about SIEM load can be answered with data rather than assurances — and it shows plainly that repeat views cost the Data Indexer nothing.

Threat Universe — investigation quality and honesty. Analyze-with-AI now cites named evidence (documents, commands, per-event times) from the pulled logs instead of only counts; answers are scoped to the artifacts the analyst actually assembled rather than the whole environment; grounded follow-up suggestions appear under each answer, minted only from data already in context and retired once asked, including investigative-progression questions (was the privilege change used, is there persistence, did anything leave the network, what preceded the successful logon); traced paths are narrated hop by hop from the shared raw-log evidence between the two artifacts, with co-occurrence never described as a directed connection; and a Stop button ends a running analysis. The assistant also renders tables and lists properly and highlights artifact names in-line.

Threat Universe fixes. Expanding an artifact that reached the canvas through another artifact's cached pull now renders its activity instead of silently drawing nothing; deep links from Alarm Investigation resolve alarms that fall outside the 3,000-node display cap by narrowing the window around the alarm automatically; a canvas click during an AI answer no longer discards that answer; and Data-Indexer case notes are formatted for reading.

No database migration. Pull the 1.2.23 app image and recreate the app container. The audit trail is ON by default and syslog forwarding is OFF until you set a host, so the upgrade changes nothing on your network until you configure it. The Ollama pin (0.20.6), RhythmAI:9b model, prompts and context budgets are unchanged.

summary: Threat Universe keeps your investigation trail
AI analysis reads as a kill-chain story
Honest IP reputation in triage briefs
No action required — update the Chrome extension
highlights: Threat Universe — investigation continuity. The detail panel now navigates like an investigation instead of a stack of dead ends: clicking any artifact (from a chip, a brief row, or the canvas) leaves a 'Back to alarm details' trail with the alarm as home base; returning restores the triage brief instantly (no rebuild click); artifact panels open directly on raw-log context that was already pulled this session — log count, cache age, and every activity chip — instead of re-offering a pull that already ran; panel chips now mirror the canvas exactly (every pulled event/host/user/IP renders, not a top-3 cut); the MITRE technique wall collapses behind a one-line summary; and the risk filter wears live per-severity alarm-count badges.

Analyze with AI — the investigation as a story. highlights: Alarm & Incident Investigation runaway fixed at the ROOT: the Ollama runtime is now pinned to 0.20.6 in every shipped compose file. Field report from an Ubuntu / NVIDIA A10 customer site: every AI investigation 'spun forever', streaming endless repeating/gibberish text and never completing (the analyst had to hit Stop each time). Root cause confirmed by A/B reproduction on identical inputs -- same RhythmAI:9b model digest (20ac65dc7ba0), same prompts, same sampling parameters, with ONLY the Ollama runtime changed: Ollama 0.20.6 produced 0 runaways across a 13-alarm batch, while Ollama 0.30.10 produced 12 runaways across the same 13 (0% -> 92%). The trigger was the floating `ollama/ollama:latest` image tag: the customer's fresh install pulled 0.30.10, a runtime with a generation regression that prevents RhythmAI:9b from emitting its end-of-sequence token, so it generates all the way to the num_predict cap (~7.5 minutes on an A10). Validated deployments had been running the older 0.20.6 via the same `latest` tag pulled months earlier, which is why the behavior was never seen in-house. The model, prompts, and parameters are byte-identical across both versions -- the regression lives entirely in the Ollama runtime/sampler. Fix: all compose files (Windows installer, Ubuntu installer, and deploy variants) now pin `ollama/ollama:0.20.6` instead of `latest`, permanently eliminating the version drift for every future install.

Server-side runaway watchdog added to Alarm & Incident Investigation as defense-in-depth. Independently of the Ollama pin, the streaming generation loop now inspects output as it is produced (about once every 1,500 characters -- negligible cost) and stops a degenerate generation that would otherwise run to the ~24K-token cap. It detects visible output exceeding 40,000 characters (healthy reports are 2-4K), a report section header repeating (section cycling), near-zero text diversity in the tail (token loops), low line diversity (phrase loops), and an unclosed reasoning block exceeding 32,000 characters. On a trip it finalizes gracefully -- keeping any usable partial report with a truncation note, or showing a clear 'investigation stopped, please re-run' message -- so the UI never hangs on 'Analyzing...'. Validated on 14 real reports (densest alarms up to 334 correlations, largest incidents up to 6,216 aggregated alarms): zero false positives, ~10-12x headroom over the largest legitimate report. With Ollama pinned the watchdog should rarely fire; it exists to bound any residual or future runaway, not to prevent it.

Coverage AI Assistant (Rhythm Insights chat) now has the same runaway watchdog. The same A10 site hit a separate, related failure: a strategic coverage question ('which users trigger the most alarms -- is this normal or concerning?') spiraled inside the model's reasoning block and hung for 5+ minutes ('Thinking...' forever) until the analyst cancelled it. Unlike the alarm runaway this is NOT the Ollama version -- it happens on the validated 0.20.6 runtime -- it is the heavy coverage system prompt driving the small model to over-reason on open-ended/strategic questions. The factual router (v1.2.18) already shields the common factual questions by serving them straight from Postgres with no LLM; this release extends the watchdog to the coverage chat streaming path with coverage-calibrated ceilings (think 12,000 chars / visible 16,000 chars; the alarm section-header check is disabled since coverage answers don't use those headers). When a coverage question spirals, the watchdog now cuts it within seconds and the existing no-think rescue produces a real answer -- or, if nothing usable comes back, a clear 'analysis stopped, ask a more specific question' message -- instead of a 5-minute hang. Pressure-tested on dev against 9 real strategic/compliance/analytical coverage questions: zero false positives, largest legitimate answer 3,104 chars (~5x headroom under the ceiling). num_predict for coverage stays at 24,576 (load-bearing for long compliance answers, set v1.2.6) -- the watchdog is selective (it cuts only degenerate output), not a blunt length cap.

No database migration. For new installs, `docker compose pull` + recreate is sufficient and the Ollama pin applies automatically. Deployments already hit by the runaway (those that pulled `ollama/ollama:latest` and received 0.30.10) get immediate relief by pinning their Ollama image to 0.20.6 and recreating ONLY the ollama container -- the model and all data persist in the Docker volume, so there is no app reinstall and no model re-download. The app image (watchdog backstop) is the only code change in this release; the RhythmAI:9b model, system prompts, context window, and num_predict budget are all unchanged from 1.2.18.

highlights: Rhythm Insights AI Assistant — Coverage Analysis factual router. Six common question patterns are now answered directly from the pre-aggregated Postgres tables (which v1.2.5 originally designed for this purpose) instead of going through the LLM. The demo's canonical failing question — 'How many critical or high-risk alarms do I have today?' — went from 234 seconds of `<think>`-storm with a no-think fallback rescue down to a deterministic sub-second answer that always cites the same numbers the dashboard does. The routed patterns: (1) alarm counts by severity and time window ('how many critical alarms today', 'how many high-risk alarms in the last 24 hours'), (2) alarm volume by severity for a time window ('alarm volume by severity for the last 7 days'), (3) overall coverage score and categories covered ('what's my overall coverage score'), (4) log source health counts ('how many unhealthy log sources'), (5) rule status counts including the enabled-but-silent figure ('how many enabled rules', 'how many enabled but silent rules'), (6) bounded list of lowest-scoring rules with an optional threshold ('list rules with composite score below 30', 'show me the lowest-scoring rules' — capped at 15 rows per the formatting consistency rule). Answer shape scales with question specificity — a sharp question like 'how many critical alarms today' returns a single sentence with the count and a 90-day baseline comparison, while broader questions like 'show me alarm volume by severity' render the full 4-row × 4-time-window table. Each routed answer streams the same SSE event sequence the LLM path uses (progress, content, suggestions, token_usage, done) so the UI behavior is identical from the analyst's perspective — same progress bar, same suggested follow-up prompts at the bottom, same token usage indicator. Strategic questions, compound questions ('which rules generate the most alarms but have low quality scores'), per-rule analysis, multi-turn follow-ups, and anything the router doesn't have a pattern for continue to flow through the LLM exactly as in v1.2.17. The router is gated on `isCoverageAnalysis=true`, so Alarm Investigation, Incident Investigation, the standalone AI Assistant, and the Chrome extension popup are completely untouched. Errors in the router (Postgres unavailable, unexpected data shape) fall through to the LLM path — graceful degradation. Closes the v1.2.16 → v1.2.17 trace finding that the 9B's `<think>`-storm pattern on factual questions wasn't a framework-count problem (dev with 4 frameworks reproduced demo's 10-framework failure identically); the actual mechanism is the 21-rule system prompt becoming a compliance checklist the model audits 800+ times per response. Routing the question out of the LLM eliminates that whole class of failure for the most common analyst workflow (open Assistant, ask one factual lookup, close).

MITRE technique-ID hallucination loop closed for the 'list rules below score X' question class. When asked to list low-scoring rules, the 9B was falling into an autoregressive pattern-continuation attractor — once a few real rules with MITRE-format names appeared in the output ('T1057:Process Discovery', 'T1078.002:Domain Accounts'), the model's sampling locked onto the pattern 'T<incrementing-number>:<cycling-technique-name>' and emitted fabricated entries (verified case: T1525 → T3787, roughly 2,260 fake MITRE techniques that don't exist in the real catalog). repeat_penalty=1.3 doesn't catch this because each line is technically a different string. Router pattern 6 ('list rules with composite score below X' / 'show me the lowest-scoring rules' / 'rules with low quality scores') now serves a bounded 15-row table from the rules aggregate with rank, name, composite score, quality score, FP risk, and 90-day alarm count — no LLM, no autoregressive surface, no hallucination. Tested on dev with the question that originally triggered the loop ('list all rules with composite score below 30') and confirmed: 200 matching rules detected, lowest 15 shown, sub-second response, all rule names match the database. The compound 'most alarms + low quality' intersection question still flows through the LLM (the router's anti-match keeps it from intercepting cross-table reasoning), and the LLM handles that question type cleanly since the alarm-count constraint bounds the answer space.

Answer-length proportional to question specificity. Earlier router output always rendered the full severity × time-window table for any alarm-count question, which felt heavy-handed for a one-cell question. The handler now branches on what the user actually asked: specific severity + specific time ('how many critical alarms today') → one-line answer with the count; specific severity + no time ('how many critical alarms') → that severity across all four windows in a single line; all severities + specific time ('alarm volume in the last 7 days') → severity breakdown for that window in a single line; broad query without any qualifier ('alarm volume by severity') → the full 4-row × 4-time-window reference table. Every variant ends with one sentence comparing the relevant window's volume to the 90-day daily or weekly baseline, marked with 'elevated activity', 'quieter than usual', or 'in line with' depending on the ratio.

The factual router is purely additive (new module, new constructor parameter, new chat_streaming early-return); the system prompt is unchanged; the LLM path is unchanged for anything the router doesn't intercept. Customers who never hit one of the six routed question patterns will see identical behavior to v1.2.17. Customers who DO ask the failing question will see it answered in sub-second time instead of 234 seconds, with the same numbers the dashboard shows.

highlights: Rhythm Insights background worker now defers its LLM-heavy steps when a user chat is in flight. The v1.2.13/1.2.14 metrics showed that the demo customer's intermittent `<think>`-storm pattern (24K-token reasoning, no-think fallback, 5-10 minute coverage chat waits) lined up with the insights worker's daily Tier C tick firing concurrent LLM calls against Ollama's `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=2` slots. With both slots busy and the worker holding one, the user chat's KV cache could get partially evicted mid-generation, sending the model into a reasoning loop until it hit num_predict, then dropping to the no-think fallback that produced the visibly-degraded final answers. A new `InvestigationService._active_user_chats` counter is now bumped at the start of every user-facing streaming method (alarm investigation, incident investigation, AI Assistant chat) and decremented in `finally`. The insights worker reads `InvestigationService.is_user_chat_active()` before kicking off any of its 4 LLM-heavy steps — auto-classify (5-min tick), rule quality assessment, LLM contextual recommendations, and executive summary (all 24-hour tick). If a user chat is mid-flight, the worker logs an INFO line and defers the step; the auto-classify retries on the next 5-min outer cycle, and the entire daily Tier C block defers as a unit (maximum 5-minute wait after the user finishes chatting). Non-LLM steps in the worker — composite score calculation, coverage recalculation, gap snapshots, template recommendations, log source sync, entity sync — are unaffected and continue running on schedule. Net effect: customers who keep the AI Assistant open for an extended Q&A session no longer see worker-driven slot contention disrupt their chat quality. The fix is intentionally pessimistic (any active chat defers any worker LLM call) since the contention symptom is severe and the deferral cost is small. Single-process asyncio, atomic int operations, no lock needed.

Also useful for spotting performance regressions across releases. No functional change to any code path — purely additive observability for ops + Hassan + customers debugging slow chats. The log line is at INFO level so it's visible without changing log verbosity.
No database migration. Direct `docker compose pull` + container recreate is sufficient — no customer action required.

summary: Much faster first answer from the AI Assistant
Alarm investigations no longer finish empty
