No action required
highlights: Rhythm Insights AI Assistant first-response time dropped from ~5-7 minutes to ~5-15 seconds for follow-up questions, and ~30-60 seconds for the very first question after opening the panel. When a customer opens the Assistant from Rhythm Insights, a new 'Optimizing AI assistant — first time setup takes about 30 seconds' banner appears while the backend pre-warms Ollama's KV cache with the full coverage context (a new POST /api/insights/assistant/prewarm endpoint sends a tiny num_predict=4 completion that walks Ollama through prompt processing for the ~30-60K token coverage dataset). By the time the user reads the welcome message and clicks a suggested prompt, the model has the prompt fully cached server-side and only needs to think + answer. The send button, suggested-prompt chips, and message input are visually disabled with an 'Ask anything... (preparing assistant)' placeholder during the warmup so analysts don't fire a question before the cache is populated. A 90-second soft-unlock allows the gate to be overridden to the existing slow path if needed (rare — most prewarms complete in 10-15 seconds). Closing the modal mid-prewarm aborts the in-flight HTTP request via an AbortController, freeing the Ollama slot for other workloads. No customer-facing configuration; the prewarm fires automatically on every Assistant open.

Rhythm Insights Coverage Analysis context window raised from 32K to 64K tokens (and auto-scales to 128K for very large coverage datasets above ~49K estimated prompt tokens). Previously, generation on top of large coverage prompts could exceed the 32K window, causing Ollama's rolling-window eviction to drop the system prompt mid-thinking; the model would lose its formatting instructions, get stuck in a <think>-loop, and trigger the no-think fallback (which loses reasoning quality and produces lower-grade answers). The new 64K floor (~4.4 GB KV cache on the 9B model) keeps the system prompt alive throughout generation regardless of how long the <think> block runs. Fits comfortably on the 32 GB customer minimum GPU with OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=2 (total ~14 GB residency). Coverage paths now use their own ChatOllama instance (isolated from the 32K default that alarm investigation and worker LLM calls use), so the customer's configured `context_window` in backend/config.json no longer affects coverage mode — coverage always picks at least 64K. Token estimation in the auto-scaler was also tightened from 4 chars/token to 3 chars/token to reflect the actual density of markdown-heavy coverage content.

Alarm and Incident Investigation generation budget raised from the Ollama default 4K to 24K tokens (matches Coverage Analysis from v1.2.6 and the worker-path bumps from v1.2.9). Investigating alarms with 50+ correlated events was exhausting the 4K budget inside the model's <think> block on RhythmAI:9b and emitting nothing visible to the analyst — the investigation progress UI showed 'Investigation Complete' but the chat area stayed empty. The 24K cap gives the fine-tuned model enough headroom to both reason through dense correlation chains AND emit the formatted executive-summary + MITRE TTP + IoCs + recommendations report. Customers running RhythmAI on noisy SIEMs (multi-stage attack chains, lateral-movement clusters) will see alarm investigations actually produce output instead of silently completing with no answer. think=True is preserved — the fine-tuned model still reasons explicitly, just with more headroom.

VRAM freed immediately when the Rhythm Insights AI Assistant closes. A long-standing path bug — the release-context endpoint was being called from the frontend with an incorrect '/api/' prefix (POST /api/ai-analyst/release-context), which returned HTTP 405 Method Not Allowed silently swallowed by .catch() — meant the 9B model stayed resident in VRAM for Ollama's full 5-minute default keep_alive after every coverage chat session. On customer 32 GB GPUs running RhythmAI alongside the Regex Builder (qwen2.5-coder:32b, ~22 GB resident), this 5-minute hold was blocking the larger coder model from loading. The frontend now calls the correct path (/ai-analyst/release-context without the /api/ prefix), Ollama receives a keep_alive=0 request that forces immediate model eviction, and VRAM is freed in under 1 second of clicking the close X. Duplicate-call elimination: a second release-context POST that was also firing from a useEffect in AIAssistant.tsx has been removed — the parent close handler in RhythmInsights.tsx is now the single source of truth for the release call.

No database migration this release. Direct `docker compose pull` + container recreate is sufficient — no customer action required, no re-classification needed. The Rhythm Insights AI Assistant pre-warm behavior is automatic on every modal open; the 64K coverage context and 24K alarm investigation budgets are applied automatically. Customers upgrading from any prior 1.x version go directly to 1.2.12 (no intermediate-version stepping required).

summary: Drilldown backfill no longer stalls on dead alarms
Database migration runs automatically on startup
No action required
highlights: Drilldown backfill worker no longer gets stuck on permanent zombie alarms. The worker queries alarms with empty drilldown_logs to fetch from LogRhythm's DrillDownResults table, but with the previous ORDER BY date_inserted DESC the same 50 newest empty-drilldown alarms got revisited every 60-second cycle — and many of them are alarms LogRhythm will never populate (parser failures, retired log sources, transient conditions). Old alarms in the queue with potentially-usable data never got reached. Two changes: (1) flipped to ORDER BY date_inserted ASC so the worker drains the backlog chronologically; (2) added a per-alarm backfill_attempts counter (new column on alarm_drilldown_logs, migration 002). After 5 unsuccessful cycles an alarm retires from the retry loop, freeing the worker to advance through the queue. Database migration runs automatically on startup. Existing alarms get backfill_attempts=0 (DEFAULT 0 on the new column), so the 4,598-alarm zombie backlog observed at v1.2.10 deploy time will get fresh chance under the new ASC ordering and then progressively retire if SIEM still has nothing. Net: customer SIEMs whose drilldown population is flaky no longer have their backfill worker stuck pointlessly hammering the same zombies forever — the worker actually advances through the queue.

Observability: when alarms hit the backfill_attempts cap and retire from the retry loop, the worker logs an INFO line with the count and a sample of alarm IDs. Ops can correlate to specific LogRhythm rules that aren't producing drilldown and either fix the parser or accept the loss.

Direct upgrade from any prior 1.x version supported — no intermediate-version stepping required. v1.2.11 ships the first formal database migration in RhythmAI's history (migration 002 adds the backfill_attempts column). It runs automatically on container startup and is safe in all upgrade paths: (a) ADD COLUMN with DEFAULT 0 is metadata-only on PostgreSQL 11+, so it completes in milliseconds regardless of how many alarm rows you have; (b) the IF NOT EXISTS guard makes the migration idempotent — safe to re-apply if a previous run was interrupted; (c) the down() function cleanly drops the column if you need to roll back to 1.2.10 or earlier; (d) the migration runner self-bootstraps its tracking table (schema_migrations), so customers upgrading from pre-1.2.3 versions that never had the migration system don't need to do anything special — just point docker-compose at the 1.2.11 image and restart. Verify with: `docker compose logs app | grep 'Migration 002 applied successfully'` (should appear once on first startup after the upgrade).

highlights: Incident title generation: singleton incidents (one alarm) no longer call the LLM — the alarm rule name IS the title. Previously, every singleton incident created by the alarm_sync and drilldown_backfill workers triggered an LLM title-generation call. About 25% of these failed silently with the 9B model returning an empty response after a long <think> block — the model would reason its way to 'no attack pattern to title' for small/simple prompts, exhaust the 16K-token budget on thinking, then emit EOS with no answer. The empty-response retry path (retry at 32K → no-think fallback → error) burned ~5-7 minutes of GPU per failed singleton and produced the generic 'Security Incident - 1 Related Alarms' fallback anyway. The fix: bypass the LLM for singletons entirely (rule name is descriptive enough on its own) and only call the LLM for multi-alarm incidents where cross-rule synthesis is genuinely useful. Customers with active SIEMs running heavy alarm volume will see backfill catch-up time drop from days to minutes, GPU stay cool when the app is idle, and singleton incident titles become more readable (e.g., 'Lateral: Account Added to Admin Group' instead of 'Security Incident - 1 Related Alarms'). Multi-alarm incident titles are unchanged — they still get the rich LLM-synthesized titles describing the attack pattern across stitched alarms.

Incident title generation: defensive guard against oversize LLM prompts. If aggregated incident context exceeds 100,000 characters (roughly 25K tokens, leaving headroom for thinking and answer in the 9B model's 32K context window), the LLM call is skipped and a generic title is used. The aggregation helper normally produces output well below this threshold (3 alarms per rule × 5 deduplicated logs per alarm × 5 fields per log), but the guard prevents catastrophic GPU burn if any of those caps get bumped up in the future or if drilldown payloads are unusually large. An INFO-level log line records when the guard trips, so ops can correlate to specific incidents.
